NEW DELHI: Karnataka Police on Sunday registered an FIR against former BJP MP Pratap Simha and others over an alleged provocative speech made during a Ganesha idol procession in T Narasipura, Mysuru.The FIR was registered at the T Narasipura police station following a complaint by a police sub-inspector, who alleged that Simha made derogatory remarks over a microphone targeting Inspector Dhananjay during Friday’s procession.The procession and idol immersion were held amid tight security.The FIR comes amid a controversy over a reported warning by the T Narasipura town police inspector to organisers installing Ganesha idols in public ahead of the festival. The inspector had reportedly asked them not to burst crackers in front of a mosque during the idol procession, triggering protests by opposition parties.Reacting to the FIR, Simha alleged that he had been booked under pressure from Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge and said he would approach the court.“I, too, got to know about the FIR through the media. Why has an FIR been registered? If an FIR has been registered for inciting, who was inciting? It was the inspector who did it.An FIR should have been filed against him,” Simha told reporters.He alleged that the inspector had instigated the situation and made derogatory remarks against those following “Hindutvavadis”.“We have respect for the police department, and there are several good officers here in Mysuru. Why have such a person among them? An FIR should have been filed against the inspector, and action should be taken against him,” he said.Simha further claimed that 21 FIRs had previously been registered against him and that the latest case was the 22nd.“We know who the Home minister is. Under pressure from him, the FIR has been filed... Twenty-one FIRs have been filed against me; this is the 22nd. All cases against me are on Hindutva and nationalist issues... I will go to court and seek justice,” he said.
Article Summary: Karnataka Police register an FIR against former BJP MP Pratap Simha over an alleged provocative speech made during a Ganesha idol procession. Simha alleged that he had been booked under pressure from Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge and said he would approach the court.

And somehow, by the end of that extraordinary day, a spoonful of milk had become a global story.

Thirty-one years ago, on September 21, 1995, I came home from school to find that something was strangely different. My aunt, who would diligently wait for me every day and was always the one to serve me lunch, was missing. She was more than just the person who fed me; she would sit with me, tell me interesting stories and make the afternoon feel special.I looked for her everywhere. Finally, the housemaid arrived with my plate of dal and rice and casually told me, “Didi has gone to feed milk to Lord Ganesha.”I was puzzled. What did she mean? After lunch, I called a friend from the landline. She had the same story. Her mother, too, was not at home. By evening, my aunt returned, visibly excited, and told my mother, who had just come back from work, what she had seen.“I took a spoon of milk to feed Ganesha, and the milk disappeared,” she said. My mother looked at her in disbelief. “Really?” she asked. “Really. I saw it with my own eyes,” she insisted, quite overwhelmed with emotions.The news spread fast, Ganesha idols were apparently drinking milk. There were no smartphones, social media platforms, WhatsApp groups or instant notifications to amplify the news.India’s internet had only just arrived, television was still dominated by Doordarshan, and newspapers remained the primary source of next-day news. Yet, within hours, temples were overflowing, milk was disappearing from shops and the story had travelled beyond India.It was not the age of viral news. In fact viral was the world synonymous with just one thing-the infectious disease of influenza. There was no way to immediately search the internet, watch a viral video or check social media posts from another city. Then what caused the spread of this frenzy? According to a contemporary Times of India report Mumbai and several other parts of India were swept by reports that Ganesha idols were accepting milk offerings. The report described the news as spreading “like wildfire” as thousands of devotees rushed to temples.The crucial point was that people did not merely hear the claim. They went to temples and tried it for themselves. Devotees carried spoons filled with milk towards the trunks or mouths of Ganesha idols, and many reported seeing the milk disappear.The episode becomes even more extraordinary when viewed against India's technological landscape in 1995. Public internet access had only just been launched by VSNL in August that year. According to historicalinternet use in India in 1995 stood at just 0.026% of the population.Telephones were also far from universal. India had approximately 11.98 million fixed telephone connections in 1995, equivalent to around 1.24 fixed lines per 100 people.This meant that the mechanisms of mass communication were fundamentally different from those available today. A person could call a relative, but there was no instant group messaging system through which hundreds of people could receive the same information simultaneously. News moved through conversations, local networks, religious communities, radio, television and newspapers. And yet the Ganesha story moved extraordinarily quickly.It would be inaccurate to suggest that India had only Doordarshan in 1995. The country's television landscape had already begun changing. Zee TV had launched in 1992, Star TV had entered the Indian market in 1991 and Sony Entertainment Television launched in 1995. But the explosion of private, round-the-clock news channels that would later transform India's news culture was still years away.Doordarshan nevertheless remained hugely influential . An academic study citing Ministry of Information & Broadcasting figures puts India's television universe in 1995 at approximately 40 million television households and 250 million viewers.There was therefore a very different relationship between an event and the news cycle. Newspapers generally reported what had happened the previous day, television had scheduled programming rather than today's constant breaking-news stream, and there was no digital ecosystem continuously refreshing itself. The Ganesha phenomenon had to travel through people before it could become a mass media story.The reports quickly produced visible consequences. A contemporary Los Angeles Times repor published on September 23, 1995, said millions of Indians had rushed to test the phenomenon and reported that milk had “virtually disappeared” from shops in New Delhi by noon.That detail captures the extraordinary feedback loop created by the phenomenon. People heard that Ganesha was drinking milk, went out to buy milk, took it to temples and offered it to idols. The resulting rush itself became evidence of how seriously the story was being taken.Contemporary reports described crowds gathering at temples, with devotees carrying spoons, bowls and containers of milk.The most remarkable part of the episode was perhaps how quickly it crossed India's borders. Reports soon emerged from Hindu communities in Britain, the United States, Canada, Nepal and elsewhere. A contemporary os Angeles Times report noted that the reports had spread beyond India to Hindu communities in other countries, including Britain and Los Angeles. Hinduism Today later recalled receiving telephone calls and fax messages from different parts of the world reporting similar experiences. Its contemporary account provides a fascinating glimpse into how an international religious community communicated before email, social media and messaging apps became commonplace.The technology may appear primitive by today's standards, but the human network was remarkably effective. Someone in India could telephone a relative abroad, that person could contact a local temple, and within hours another community could be trying the same experiment.The story did not need an algorithm to travel. It travelled through relationships.As the reports spread, scientists and sceptics began examining what devotees were observing. One of the principal scientific explanations involved capillary action and surface tension. Rather than the idol literally consuming the milk, the liquid could move along the surface of the material, creating the appearance that it was being absorbed by the idol.For devotees, however, the scientific explanation did not necessarily invalidate what they had experienced. The same physical observation could be interpreted through very different frameworks: as a religious sign by believers, as a scientific phenomenon by researchers, and as an extraordinary mass social event by journalists.Looking back from the age of smartphones, the 1995 episode is remarkable not simply because of what people believed they were seeing, but because of how quickly the information travelled.India's public internet had only just begun. Fixed telephone connections were limited, television was expanding but had not yet become the 24-hour news environment of today, and newspapers operated on a fundamentally different news cycle. Yet within hours, a local report had become a national phenomenon and then an international story.A telephone call led to another telephone call. A conversation at one temple led to another. Newspapers carried the story forward, television added another layer of coverage and international media transformed what had begun as a local religious phenomenon into a global news story.Calling the Ganesha milk episode the world's first viral phenomenon would be too absolute. Stories travelled internationally long before 1995, through newspapers, radio, television and word of mouth.But the episode offers a remarkable case study of mass communication before the social-media era. Millions of people participated in the same rapidly spreading story without having access to the tools that today make such mass participation almost instantaneous.That is what makes September 21, 1995, worth remembering 31 years later. The question is no longer simply whether Ganesha idols were actually drinking milk. The episode has another story to tell, about technology, faith, communication and human networks.In 2026, information can travel around the world in seconds. In 1995, it travelled from person to person, from telephone to telephone, from temple to temple and eventually from newspaper to newspaper.(All images are AI Generated)
Article Summary: A spoonful of milk had become a global story in September 1995. India's internet had only just arrived, television was still dominated by Doordarshan. There was no way to immediately search the internet, watch a viral video or check social media posts from another city.

Article Title: 'Method of disenfranchising Indians': Kharge slams SIR, calls it a 'Frankenstein monster'
Article Text:
Congress leader Mallikarjun Kharge has lambasted the Election Commission's electoral roll revision, labeling it a misguided 'Frankenstein Monster' that adversely affects its constituents

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Monday stepped up his attack on the Election Commission ’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, describing the exercise as a “Frankenstein Monster” after several prominent political and government figures were issued notices in Delhi.“What started as SIR from Bihar has now knocked on Delhi’s door, and perhaps now the powers-that-be are realizing why the Congress Party has been calling the entire process flawed from day one!” Kharge said in a post on X.“SIR is not just a tool used by the BJP for vote theft and dismantling democracy, it’s a flawed process that has turned into a Frankenstein Monster, now trapping its own people!!”Kharge referred to notices issued to BJP veteran Lal Krishna Advani, external affairs minister S Jaishankar, former vice-president Jagdeep Dhankhar, Delhi Lieutenant Governor, Rajya Sabha members, former Union ministers and other prominent figures. He also referred to an earlier controversy involving Bharat Ratna-winning scientist C N R Rao and former Navy chief Admiral Arun Prakash.The Congress president also questioned the Election Commission’s reference to “VIP/marked electors”, linking it to the constitutional principle of equal voting rights.“Is there now some Special Category of voters in India’s Universal Adult Franchise, VIP voters and ordinary voters?” Kharge asked. “Isn’t this a violation of the constitutional principle of One Person, One Vote, One Value? Has the VIP vote become more valuable now?”Kharge also cited the situation in West Bengal, where Election Commission data submitted before the Supreme Court showed that 1,26,194 appeals against exclusion had been decided.Of these, 1,13,943 voters were ordered to be restored to the electoral rolls, while 8,649 appeals were rejected. Kharge highlighted the fact that around 93 percent of the decided appeals had resulted in restoration.The figure, however, relates only to appeals decided so far and does not mean that 93 percent of all excluded voters were found to have been wrongly removed. More than 37 lakh appeals remained pending, according to the Election Commission data.SIR is an intensive revision of electoral rolls in which election officials verify existing electors and identify entries requiring correction, deletion or further verification. The exercise was first conducted in Bihar before being expanded to other states and Union territories. The process has faced political opposition and legal scrutiny over the verification criteria, documents required and safeguards available to voters.In Delhi, the draft electoral roll published on August 31 contained around 97.5 lakh electors. Around 33.13 lakh voters were identified for notices after their records could not be mapped to the previous intensive revision or were flagged for what officials described as logical discrepancies. More than 31.63 lakh notices had been served as of Sunday.Among those flagged were Advani, Jaishankar, Dhankhar, Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, AAP leader Arvind Kejriwal, former deputy chief minister Manish Sisodia and several senior officials. Some cases have already been cleared after documents were verified.The Delhi CEO has maintained that receiving an SIR notice does not mean deletion from the electoral roll. The notices form part of the verification process, and voters are allowed to submit documents and make representations before any decision is taken. The final electoral roll is scheduled to be published on November 4.
Article Summary: Congress leader Mallikarjun Kharge has lambasted the Election Commission's electoral roll revision. He described the exercise as a misguided 'Frankenstein Monster' that adversely affects its constituents. Kharge referred to notices issued to BJP veteran Lal Krishna Advani, external affairs minister S Jaishankar, former vice-president Jagdeep Dhankhar.

Article Title: Kejriwal, Sisodia, Sanjay Singh get 4 weeks to reply in Delhi HC contempt case
Article Text:
The Delhi High Court will hear a criminal contempt case against AAP leaders on November 16

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court on Monday listed for hearing on November 16 a criminal contempt case against AAP leaders Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia, Sanjay Singh and others over allegedly “vilifying” social media posts targeting Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma.A bench of Justices Navin Chawla and Arun Bhardwaj granted Kejriwal and the other accused four weeks to file their replies.Kejriwal’s senior counsel told the court that he was yet to receive the complete material on the basis of which the contempt proceedings were initiated. The bench directed the registry to provide the material, which was stated to be incomplete.“Reply, if any, to be filed in four weeks,” the bench said.The court also listed for November 16 a separate contempt petition filed by lawyer Ashok Chaitanya against Kejriwal and others, including AAP leader Gopal Rai and journalist Saurav Das. The petition alleges that they were part of an “orchestrated social media campaign” against Justice Sharma.Justice Sharma had initiated criminal contempt proceedings on May 14 against Kejriwal, Sisodia, Singh and other AAP leaders, including Durgesh Pathak, Saurabh Bharadwaj and Vinay Mishra, over allegedly “vilifying” social media posts concerning her handling of the Delhi excise policy case.Contempt proceedings were also initiated against X user Devesh Vishwakarma.It was further noted the circulation of clips from court proceedings and said the proposed contemnors were attempting to create a “parallel narrative”. She observed that “remaining silent” in such circumstances would not amount to judicial restraint but a “surrender before a powerful litigant”.The contempt proceedings stem from the excise policy case. On February 27, a trial court discharged Kejriwal, Sisodia and 21 others, holding that the prosecution’s case could not withstand judicial scrutiny.
Article Summary: The Delhi High Court will hear a criminal contempt case against AAP leaders on November 16. Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma had initiated criminal contempt proceedings on May 14 against Kejriwal, Sisodia, Singh and other AAP leaders. The court also listed for November 16 a separate contempt petition filed by lawyer Ashok Chaitanya.

Article Title: IIT-Bombay student suicide case: Institute apologises over earlier remarks; student affairs dean suspended
Article Text:
IIT Bombay suspends Dean Suryanarayana Doolla

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

MUMBAI: IIT-Bombay placed Prof Suryanarayana Doolla on immediate suspension from his deanship, following continued students' protests on campus for the last three days. Prof Doolla was the dean of administrative affairs. He was accused of abetment of Sahil Wakode's death by suicide. Wakode's family also filed a case of harassment against him under the Atrocities Act. The institute issued a public apology on their social media handle, after students accused them of 'defaming' Wakode, without carrying out a detailed inquiry."We apologise for the statements contained in our earlier communication concerning the circumstances surrounding the unfortunate demise of Sahil," it said. "The details and circumstances leading up to the incident remain subject to investigation by the appropriate authorities. In view of the ongoing investigation, it was inappropriate to have set out or characterised details relating to the events preceding his demise before they had been duly established through the appropriate investigative process," the institute added. The administration also denied the allegations of the director's resignation, after videos of him from the protest went viral.In a mail sent to the campus residents, the institute director, Prof Shireesh Kedare, mentioned, 'the deanship of Prof Suryanarayan Doolla is suspended with immediate effect. Any further action will be taken after investigation'. Doolla has not been suspended from his professorship at the energy science and engineering department.A meeting of the institute's Board of Governors is underway.The students submitted a charter of 18 demands on Sunday night in a meeting with the director and the institute functionaries, which went on for three hours. The director signed the charter. Students pressed on the suspension of Prof Doolla and an apology along with 16 other demands.In the list of demands raised by the students' groups on the campus, the students have demanded an an independent investigation committee, with student representatives and external members recommended by students, suspension of officials who are found guilty after the investigation, a fair compensation for the families.Among the many demands, the students have also sought a code of conduct and sensitisation for professors.The director signed the list of demands on the live recording, though officials refused to comment. An open house with students is expected to be scheduled today.Protests erupted on the Powai campus on Friday night after Wakode, a second-year student of energy science and engineering, ended his life hours after he was caught using a mobile phone during the institute’s mid-semester examination. He allegedly uploaded the exam paper on an AI platform for answers. This is the third case of suicide on the campus this year.While the institute, in a statement, mentioned that no action was initiated against Wakode, many claimed that he was threatened with suspension.
Article Summary: IIT Bombay suspends Dean Suryanarayana Doolla. He was accused of abetment of Sahil Wakode's death by suicide. The students submitted a charter of 18 demands on Sunday night in a meeting with the director and the institute functionaries, which went on for three hours.

NEW DELHI: The recitation of Vande Mataram in the Karnataka Assembly ended after two stanzas, following which BJP MLAs recited the full version of the song, objecting to the decision to limit its rendition.BJP MLA SR Vishwanath criticised the Congress-led Karnataka government over the issue and alleged that the move was aimed at appeasing the party’s central leadership."Even before independence, Congress opposed Vande Mataram and stopped singing it in their meetings. To please Sonia Gandhi, the Congress government in Karnataka, led by Chief Minister DK Shivakumar, brought it to the cabinet and said we will sing only two paragraphs, not the full song. To please the Congress high command, they have truncated Vande Mataram, which is equal to the national anthem. We strongly oppose this. Today, in Vidhana Soudha, if they truncate it, all BJP MLAs will sing the full Vande Mataram song, even if they try to stop us."The BJP MLAs subsequently recited the complete version of Vande Mataram in the Assembly.The Karnataka government had earlier directed that only the first two stanzas of the national song ‘Vande Mataram’ be played or sung at state government programmes and official ceremonies.According to a government order dated September 8, 2026, the decision was taken in accordance with guidelines issued by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs.The order states that, except at programmes attended by the President, Vice President, Prime Minister or Governor, only the first two stanzas of ‘Vande Mataram’ shall be sung at state government programmes.The order was issued in the name of the Governor of Karnataka.
Article Summary: The Karnataka government had earlier directed that only the first two stanzas of the national song ‘Vande Mataram’ be played or sung at state government programmes and official ceremonies. To please Sonia Gandhi, the Congress government in Karnataka, led by Chief Minister DK Shivakumar, brought it to the cabinet and said we will sing only two paragraphs.

NEW DELHI: Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra have spoken out over the alleged gang rape and murder of a teenage girl in Delhi, with both questioning the authorities over women's safety and demanding accountability for the incident.Rahul Gandhi, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha, criticised the Delhi Police and questioned the responsibility of Union home minister Amit Shah, under whose ministry the force functions. He said the teenager was gang-raped and murdered before her body was dumped in an open field, and questioned how the police remained unaware of the crime for days.In a post on X, Rahul Gandhi described the incident as a "horrific act of brutality" in the national capital. He also dismissed the idea that Delhi was providing women with a safe environment, saying the city had instead become a source of fear for women."It's unfortunate that Delhi is no longer the capital today; it has become a terrifying daily story for women," he said.Rahul directly questioned Shah over the responsibility for women's safety in Delhi. He pointed out that the Delhi Police is under the Union home ministry and asked who should ultimately be held responsible for the safety of women in the capital."Amit Shah ji, Delhi Police is under your control. Ultimately, whose responsibility is women's safety?" he said.He also criticised the functioning of the Delhi Police, asking whether its role had been reduced to intimidating ordinary citizens while criminals continued to operate without fear."Or has the job of Delhi Police been reduced to just intimidating and threatening ordinary citizens? Because the criminals are roaming around fearlessly," Gandhi said.Calling for immediate action, the Congress leader demanded that those responsible for the crime be arrested and punished strictly. He also sought accountability for what he described as criminal negligence."The beasts must be arrested immediately, strict action and punishment must be taken, and accountability for this criminal negligence must be fixed," he said.Rahul Gandhi ended his post by linking women's safety to India's wider progress, saying, "India cannot move forward without women's safety."Priyanka Gandhi also raised concerns over the case, saying the crime against the teenager represented an extreme form of brutality. She noted that another minor girl had allegedly been raped just days earlier and questioned whether authorities were taking sufficient responsibility for women's safety."In Delhi, all limits of cruelty were crossed against a 17-year-old girl, and after that, she was brutally murdered. Just a few days earlier, another minor girl was raped," she said in a post on X.Priyanka Gandhi further questioned the government's response to crimes against women. She argued that while there was discussion about women's development, women continued to face violence without what she described as concrete action against perpetrators."No one in the country is willing to take responsibility for women's safety—only empty talk about women's development is offered," she said.She claimed that hundreds of women face atrocities and violence and alleged that victims can struggle to get action from authorities, including the registration of FIRs."Hundreds of women face atrocities and violence, but they cannot hope for concrete action against the perpetrators—FIRs aren't even filed," she said.Priyanka Gandhi also said the issue went beyond the individual case and reflected a wider failure to ensure women's basic rights. She argued that both society and the government had failed to provide women with adequate safety, freedom and equality."Both society and the government have completely failed in granting women their rights to safety, freedom, and equality," she said.A teenage girl was allegedly gang-raped and murdered in Delhi. Her body was subsequently dumped in an open field, with the police facing questions over the delay in detecting the crime.The case has triggered political criticism over women's safety in the capital, with Rahul Gandhi focusing on the Delhi Police's role and its accountability to the Union home ministry.Priyanka Gandhi also referred to another case involving a minor girl that was reported days before the teenager's rape and murder. She used the two incidents to question the wider response to crimes against women.
Article Summary: A teenage girl was allegedly gang-raped and murdered in Delhi. Her body was subsequently dumped in an open field. The case has triggered political criticism over women's safety in the capital. Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra have spoken out over the alleged gang rape and murder of a teenage girl.

Article Title: ‘Our generation was mentally strong’: Congress leader Shama Mohamed on IIT-B suicide case
Article Text:
The Mumbai Police has transferred the case to the Crime Branch after the student’s father filed a complaint

NEW DELHI: Congress spokesperson Shama Mohamed on Monday expressed solidarity with an IIT Bombay professor accused by the father of a second-year BTech student of harassing his son, saying that students in her generation were “mentally strong”.The student, from IIT Bombay’s Department of Energy Science and Engineering, allegedly died by suicide on Friday evening after he was found using a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination.The Mumbai Police has transferred the case to the Crime Branch after the student’s father filed a complaint alleging that IIT Bombay professor and exam invigilator Suryanarayana Doolla had hurled casteist slurs at his son over the past three months. An FIR has been registered against Doolla.Reacting to the controversy, Mohamed wrote: “In this suicide, I stand with Professor Doolla. If a student is caught cheating, it is normal to admonish him & ask him to leave the room. If the student was harassed due to his caste, he should have complained to the SC/ST department.”She added: “When we were kids - we were admonished by teachers, parents for our wrongdoings but our generation was mentally strong.”Mohamed also called for greater mental health support for students, writing: “I would request colleges to have mental health therapists for the wellbeing of the students.”According to IIT Bombay, the student was found with a mobile phone in the examination hall and had uploaded the question paper on ChatGPT to seek answers. The institute said no disciplinary action had been initiated against him.The IIT Bombay Faculty Forum has also expressed solidarity with Doolla, saying he was following institute-approved procedures after detecting the alleged academic malpractice. It said the professor reported the incident to the authorities for further action.The institute said Doolla and the Head of Department had counselled the student and assured him that the incident would not adversely affect his academic career. The student subsequently returned to his hostel room, where he was later found dead.The incident has since triggered student protests on campus, with students demanding accountability and transparency from the administration.
Article Summary: Congress spokesperson Shama Mohamed expresses solidarity with IIT Bombay professor. Suryanarayana Doolla is accused by the father of a second-year BTech student of harassing his son. The student allegedly died by suicide on Friday evening after he was found using a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination.

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sachin Pilot tore into CM Bhagwant Mann-led Punjab government after a person "consumed poisonous substance" over harassement he allegedly faced for speaking against durg menace in the poll-bound state.Highlighting the incident, which would possibly compound the crisis for the Mann government, Pilot impressed upon the lack of accountablity for such incidents."The kind of pressure and mistreatment being meted out to those raising their voices against drugs in Punjab—this incident in Sangrur is clearly demonstrating it," Sachin Pilot wrote on X.Pilot, who is also Congress party's poll incharge in Punjab, further wrote: "Resident of Namol village, Jagga Singh, consumed a poisonous substance outside the DC's office. Ever since he started posting videos against drugs, he had been receiving threats and being harassed. Amidst grand claims about a drug-free Punjab, such incidents have raised serious questions on the accountability of the AAP government and the administration. ""The ground reality is telling a completely different story—if even those raising their voices against drugs are not safe, then what kind of change are we talking about?" Pilot questioned.On the incident, Dr Iqbal Singh, Civil Hospital Sangrur, said: "We received information about a patient who had been admitted due to phenyl poisoning. Upon bringing the patient into the hospital, we checked their vital signs; the patient was irritable and in a semi-unconscious state. We administered first aid and collected a sample related to the poisoning. We also consulted with the physician, as the patient's blood pressure was slightly elevated. After providing initial treatment, the patient was referred elsewhere. We have informed the police and also brought the matter to the attention of our SMO and senior officers."A political row exploded over the suicide of a 46-year-old Sangrur farmer, an addict’s father, who expressed his pain before finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema at a public rally and asked why Punjab government was unable to rein in the drugs menace.Later, Victim Gulzar Singh’s family members allege that some villagers and police intimidated him for questioning the minister, which drove him to suicide.The incident has put the Mann government under growing pressure over its handling of Punjab's drug menace.Police registered an FIR against five persons, including the sarpanch, her husband and two panchayat members of Toor Banjara village in Cheema’s Dirba assembly constituency. They face charges of abetment to suicide and caste-based humiliation. The sarpanch’s husband denied the allegations.Opposition parties in Punjab, however, are gunning for Cheema and the AAP-led government. Congress functionary Sukhpal Singh Khaira shared a video purportedly showing Gulzar naming Cheema and others, and demanded an FIR against the minister and his associates. Shiromani Akali Dal president Sukhbir Singh Badal visited Gulzar’s family on Tuesday, and demanded an abetment-to-suicide case against Cheema. BJP made the same demand, plus a CBI probe.
Article Summary: Congress leader Sachin Pilot tore into Punjab government after a person "consumed poisonous substance" over harassement he allegedly faced for speaking against durg menace. Pilot: "The kind of pressure and mistreatment being meted out to those raising their voices against drugs in Punjab is clearly demonstrating it"

NEW DELHI: Congress on Monday targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led central government over "skyrocketing prices" of food and other commodities, using the popular Bollywood song "Kya hua tera vada" to question the PM's silence on inflation.Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report on rising prices of food items, pulses and cooking oil, and alleged that the increase was putting pressure on household budgets."The skyrocketing prices of food items in the country have broken the back of the middle and poor classes," Ramesh said in a post in Hindi. He said rising prices were making pulses and other essential food items increasingly difficult for poorer households to afford."But the Prime Minister remains silent on inflation. The country is asking, 'Where have the 'achche din' gone, Prime Minister ji?' Are they only left in sermons?" he said."The people go hungry, the government stays silent," Ramesh said, questioning whether this was the "new India".Taking a swipe at the government, Ramesh wrote, "Kya hua tera vada? Woh kasam, woh irada?", a reference to the popular song from the 1977 Bollywood film Hum Kisise Kum Nahin.Ramesh claimed that prices of several everyday commodities had risen sharply in recent months, adding to the burden on households."In the past month, spice prices have surged by a massive 10% to 25%. Green cardamom has risen from 4000 rupees to 4400 rupees/kg, black cardamom from 2400 rupees to 2800 rupees/kg, and cumin has jumped from 360 rupees to 400 rupees/kg. Mace prices have shot up directly from 2500 rupees to 3000 rupees per kg,” Jairam said."Arhar dal has increased from 100 rupees to 130 rupees/kg, chana dal from 70 rupees to 100 rupees/kg, and urad from 120 rupees to 140 rupees/kg. Mustard oil has reached 210 rupees/litre from 190 rupees, and Safola oil has climbed to 280 rupees/litre from 240 rupees," he added.Ramesh also claimed that onion prices had risen sharply between June and September. “From June to September, the all-India average retail price of onions rose from 29.50 rupees/kg to 53.78 rupees/kg - a staggering 82.3% increase in just three and a half months," he said.The Congress leader called on the Modi government to take immediate measures to address what he described as "uncontrolled inflation" and provide relief to consumers.
Article Summary: Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report on rising prices of food items, pulses and cooking oil. He said rising prices were making pulses and other essential food items increasingly difficult for poorer households to afford. The country is asking, 'Where have the 'achche din' gone, Prime Minister ji?'

Article Title: Bengal SIR tribunals may take 12 years to decide on appeals
Article Text:
SIR appeals pile up in WB, EC says hike number of tribunals

Excessive backlog

NEW DELHI: The innumerable voters in West Bengal who were removed from the electoral rolls after special intensive revision (SIR) may not be able to vote for more than a decade as appellate tribunals set up by Supreme Court could take more than 12 years to decide on their appeals for inclusion, going by the present pace of adjudication.An affidavit filed by Election Commission before Supreme Court says 1,26,194 applications have been decided by tribunals in the last five months since they started functioning in mid-April. So, on average, 25,238 cases are being decided by the tribunals in a month when even Saturdays and Sundays are included as working days. The total number of pending cases as of Sept 16, when the affidavit was filed, was 37,05,235. At current speed, if the tribunals work seven days a week, it would take 146 months to decide all cases.Admitting that the present infrastructure and number of tribunals are insufficient to handle the Herculean task of adjudicating 37 lakh cases, the poll panel pleaded with the court to increase the number of tribunals in the state from 24 to 42, almost double the present strength, and allow judicial officers to work from home."With a view to further streamlining and expediting the disposal of the pending appeals, it is proposed that the number of appellate tribunals in the state of West Bengal may be considered for increase to correspond with the number of parliamentary constituencies in the state, so as to facilitate expeditious disposal of the pending appeals," said the affidavit, filed in response to a petition from TMC MP Derek O' Brien. Allowing judicial workers to conduct hearings and undertake other proceedings from home "would assist in expediting the disposal of pending appeals by minimising the time lost in conveyance", it said.In another affidavit filed in response to a petition on the functioning of the tribunals, the commission said they were constituted pursuant to the directives of the apex court and the standard operating procedure (SOP) governing their functioning has been formulated by the committee constituted for this purpose, comprising, inter alia, former judges of the high court at Calcutta."It is humbly submitted that the reliefs sought by the petitioner pertain primarily to the functioning, procedure and accessibility of the appellate mechanism and, therefore, fall within the domain of the SOP governing the functioning of the appellate tribunals and the authorities entrusted with the administration thereof. The feasibility, modalities and implementation... are matters best left to the consideration of the concerned appellate tribunal. .." the affidavit said.
Article Summary: EC says 1,26,194 applications have been decided by tribunals in the last five months since they started functioning in mid-April. On average, 25,238 cases are being decided in a month when even Saturdays and Sundays are included as working days. Total number of pending cases as of Sept 16, when the affidavit was filed, was 37,05,235. At current speed, if the tribunal work seven days a week, it would take 146 months to decide all cases.

Article Text:
EC revised the rules in Phase 2 covering 12 states/UTs, doing away with the requirement to submit documents

NEW DELHI: The large number of notices served to electors under the special intensive revision (SIR) largely stem from a key change made to SIR instructions by the Election Commission, based on its experience during SIR Phase I in Bihar. During SIR in Bihar, the rules required electors to attach documents proving their eligibility to be included in the roll, over a dozen documents were listed as acceptable proof of birth, citizenship and residence, at the enumeration stage itself.However following the uproar over the inconvenience caused to electors who may not have had these documents and thus faced exclusion, the EC revised the rules in Phase 2 covering 12 states/UTs, doing away with the requirement to submit documents with the enumeration form (EF) and instead decided to map the electors with the electoral roll from last SIR. The mapping works with inbuilt algorithms to flag logical discrepancies between the last roll and the enumeration forms, based on which notices are automatically issued.“The logical discrepancy detecting software is agnostic and does not distinguish between a VIP and a common man. The fact that election commissioner. S S Sandhu also got a notice due a discrepancy, where his name was mentioned as S S Sandhu in one place and as Sukhbir Singh Sandhu in another, proves this,” an EC functionary pointed out.“The high number of notices seems to unique to urban centres like Delhi, where the electors may have been a little casual while filling up the EF. Also, the BLOs could have been more meticulous in checking forms at the enumeration stage, as this could have cut down the discrepancies that led to the notices,” said an EC official.“If anyone does not return the EF despite three visits of the booth level officer (BLO) to his address and checking by booth level agent (BLA) of political parties, he is either absent, shifted, dead or duplicate elector and his name is not there in draft roll. ⁠If the received EF are incomplete or gives incorrect information, notices are issued.The official added that notices rarely lead to electors’ exclusion and are resolved the moment the elector presents the proof correcting the discrepancy.“No elector is excluded without a hearing, which must be followed by a speaking order, which can, after the final roll be published, be challenged first before the district election officer and then the chief electoral officer,” said an EC official.“Besides, the option of being added back to the electoral roll remains open in perpetuity. Anyone whose name is left out can always fill up Form 6, along with the declaration, on his mobile to get back into the electoral roll,” the official added.
Article Summary: The large number of notices served to electors under the special intensive revision (SIR) largely stem from a key change made to SIR instructions by the Election Commission. During SIR in Bihar, the rules required electors to attach documents proving their eligibility to be included in the roll. EC revised the rules in Phase 2 covering 12 states/UTs, doing away with the requirement to submit documents.

Article Title: Amit Shah wants UCC in all NDA states by 2029. What will JD(U) do in Bihar?
Article Text:
What is UCC

BJP's old promise

Why UCC needs careful balancing for JD(U)

When JD(U) differed with BJP

Mahagathbandhan's offer to Nitish

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Is the implementation of the Uniform Civil Code emerging as a new point of contention between the Bharatiya Janata Party and one of its oldest allies, Janata Dal (United)?The question has come into focus after Union home minister Amit Shah's assertion that UCC would be implemented in all 21 NDA-ruled states before the next Lok Sabha elections prompted differing reactions within the JD(U).The issue surfaced after Shah, during his visit to Mumbai, put a timeline on BJP's plan to implement one of its longstanding ideological objectives before the 2029 Lok Sabha polls."Triple talaq has been abolished, giving Muslim women equal rights. We have introduced the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in several states and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029," Shah said.Shah's message, however, drew a different response from some JD(U) leaders in Bihar.JD(U) general secretary and former minister Shyam Rajak said his party did not favour implementing UCC in the state."Our stand on the issue was made clear by our leader way back. He had said that although our party was supporting the UCC Bill in the Parliament, it was not in favour of implementing the same in Bihar," Rajak said."The chief minister may be of the BJP but the government is being run with the help of allies...our stand is clear, the question of implementing UCC in Bihar does not arise," he added.However, Bihar deputy chief minister Vijay Kumar Chaudhary, who is considered to be a close ally of former chief minister Nitish Kumar, adopted a more cautious stance and said the party would first study the legislation and would not oppose it "for no reason" if its provisions were found to be unexceptionable."As of now, we are not aware of the details of the legislation on UCC. Let it be placed before us. If we find there is nothing objectionable, why shall we oppose it without any reason? And if there are points of concern, these will be conveyed to the Union home minister," Chaudhary said.JD(U) working president Sanjay Jha has also indicated that party leaders would discuss the issue with Shah.For now, therefore, JD(U)'s stand is not entirely clear. While some leaders have spoken against implementing UCC in Bihar, remarks by senior leaders such as Chaudhary and Jha have left scope for the party to examine the proposed provisions before taking a final position. The party has historically favoured wider consultations and consensus on the issue.India already has uniform criminal laws and common civil laws covering matters such as taxation, contracts and negotiable instruments. However, when it comes to personal laws such as marriage, divorce and inheritance of property, different religious communities follow laws based on their respective traditions and practices.Article 44 under the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Constitution says that the State shall endeavour to secure a UCC for citizens throughout India."The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India," the Constitution says.A UCC broadly seeks to provide a common legal framework for citizens in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and succession.The Uniform Civil Code has been a longstanding part of the BJP's political agenda and has featured repeatedly in the party's election manifestos over the years.The party has repeatedly included the issue in its election manifestos, arguing that a common civil code would ensure equality before law and strengthen women's rights in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption.Matters such as marriage, divorce, adoption, wills, intestacy and succession fall in the Concurrent List, allowing both the Centre and state governments to make laws on them.In 2022, then Union law minister Kiren Rijiju also informed the Rajya Sabha that states were empowered to legislate on these subjects."Article 44 of the Constitution provides that the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India," Rijiju had said in a written reply."Personal laws such as intestacy and succession; wills; joint family and partition; marriage and divorce, relate to Entry 5 of List-III-Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and hence, the States are also empowered to legislate upon them," he had added.This has allowed BJP-ruled states to take the state route on UCC.Uttarakhand became the first state in independent India to implement a state-specific Uniform Civil Code on January 27, 2025.Since then, UCC Bills have also been passed by the assemblies of BJP-ruled Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh. As of mid-September, the Bills in these three states were awaiting the President's assent.Other NDA-ruled states are at different stages of considering or preparing their own legislation.Shah's latest remarks have now put a 2029 timeline on that process for all NDA-ruled states.For JD(U), the issue comes with both political and ideological considerations.Nitish Kumar has long maintained that a reform such as UCC should not be pushed without broad consultation and consensus, particularly given India's social and religious diversity.There is also an electoral dimension.Within the NDA in Bihar, JD(U) has traditionally sought support across a social coalition that includes Extremely Backward Classes, women and sections of minorities. While its support among Muslims has weakened over the years, the party has continued to reach out to the community.Muslims constitute around 17.7% of Bihar's population, according to the state's caste survey. Recent electoral data cited by The Indian Express suggests that only a relatively small section of Muslim voters backed the NDA in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, underlining the challenge for JD(U) in retaining support among the community while remaining part of the BJP-led alliance.In the 2025 assembly election, JD(U) fielded four Muslim candidates, but only Mohammad Zama Khan won from the Chainpur seat.The political setting has also changed since that election.The NDA won 202 of Bihar's 243 assembly seats, with the BJP emerging as the single-largest party with 89 seats and JD(U) winning 85.Nitish Kumar is also no longer chief minister, with BJP's Samrat Choudhary now heading the NDA government. JD(U), however, remains one of its two principal constituents.This makes the UCC question an important one for the alliance: BJP has put a timeline on a longstanding policy commitment, while JD(U) has traditionally stressed consultation before any such move.Although an ally of BJP, JD(U) has not always agreed with it on politically sensitive issues.On UCC itself, Nitish Kumar has long cautioned against hurried implementation.In January 2017, as Bihar chief minister, he returned the Law Commission's questionnaire on UCC, arguing that there was insufficient clarity about what the proposed code would contain and calling for wider consultations with affected groups.Nitish argued that diverse customs and practices had existed for centuries and that any effort towards a common code should be based on consensus rather than simply imposed.JD(U) has also differed from the BJP on issues such as the Triple Talaq Bill and the abrogation of Article 370.In 2019, JD(U) opposed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Bill, commonly known as the Triple Talaq Bill. The party objected particularly to the provision making instant triple talaq a criminal offence, arguing that the legislation could create "a lack of trust" in society. Its MPs walked out of the Lok Sabha debate and later abstained during the Rajya Sabha proceedings.In August 2019, the party also opposed the Modi government's decision to abrogate the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 and reorganise the former state into two Union Territories. JD(U) MPs staged a walkout when the measures were introduced in Parliament.However, it struck a reconciliatory note later and said that once the law had come into force, it should be abided by all.These differences did not, by themselves, prevent the BJP and JD(U) from working together. The two allies have in the past maintained separate positions on some issues while continuing their political partnership.UCC could similarly depend on what form a proposed law for Bihar eventually takes and whether the allies are able to arrive at a common position.Amid the debate over UCC, Congress and Rashtriya Janata Dal have taken the opportunity to invite Nitish Kumar to join the opposition alliance.RJD MLA Bhai Virendra asked Nitish to break ties with the BJP and form a new government with its support, saying the parties shared a socialist political tradition.The RJD MLA alleged that Nitish was surrounded by people who were "hellbent on ruining his political career" and said, "We urge Nitish Kumar ji to walk out of the NDA and form a govt with our support."Former Bihar Congress president and Rajya Sabha member Akhilesh Prasad Singh also extended an invitation to Nitish to join the Mahagathbandhan, saying Nitish had long been associated with socialist politics."It is the agenda of the BJP and the RSS. Several allies of the NDA may not agree with it, and Nitish certainly should not agree with it. He has always been associated with social concerns and socialism, so I do not think he can ever agree with this," Singh said."Why would Congress have any objection to that? If he leaves, Congress will always welcome him," he added.For now, however, the differing remarks on UCC do not necessarily point to a larger crisis within the Bihar NDA.JD(U)'s final position remains open. Some of its leaders have opposed implementation in Bihar, while others have said the party should first see the proposed legislation and discuss its concerns with the BJP leadership.Shah, meanwhile, has set a clear target of introducing UCC in all NDA-ruled states before 2029.It remains to be seen whether Bihar eventually follows that roadmap and, if it does, what shape the proposed law takes after consultations between the two allies.
Article Summary: Union home minister Amit Shah's assertion that UCC would be implemented in all 21 NDA-ruled states prompted differing reactions within the JD(U) The issue surfaced after Shah put a timeline on BJP's plan to implement one of its longstanding ideological objectives before the 2029 Lok Sabha polls.

Article Title: India to make 350 kmph bullet trains by 2030, match Japan's E10
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: India will manufacture indigenous high-speed or bullet trains with a design speed of 350 kmph (B35) by 2030, matching Japan's next-generation E10 series trains that are scheduled for production the same year, according to the railway ministry's Cabinet proposal seeking approval for the revised cost of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail (MAHSR) project.Cabinet has approved the revised cost of the project at over Rs 2 lakh crore, nearly double the original estimate prepared in 2015, and the expenditure of nearly Rs 1 lakh crore escalated cost will come from budgetary support.TOI has learnt that the ministry informed the Cabinet it has initiated the process to develop B35 trains after the Japanese side conveyed in Dec 2024 that production of existing E5 series trains was being phased out. It mentions that Japan indicated that production of E10 trains would begin in 2030 and they would be ready for operations by 2034. Officials said deployment of E10 trains would be explored when they become available.The ministry has said that manufacturing of indigenous B28 high-speed trains has been taken up and India will also develop its own Bharat Train Control System (BTCS). The move mirrors China's indigenous CTCS signalling and train control system, which manages speed, spacing and safety across conventional and high-speed rail networks.As per the ministry, sharp increase in project cost from earlier Rs 1.1 lakh crore is largely due to a more than three-fold rise in land acquisition cost to about Rs 19,700 crore; a nearly 50% increase in infrastructure cost to over Rs 1 lakh crore, and around 100% escalation in spending on trains and signalling systems compared with the 2015 estimate.The current cost of the project, excluding future Japanese trains, works out to around Rs 399 crore per km.Initially, the Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor will operate with B28 trains having a design speed of 280 kmph, while their maximum operating speed will be "249 kmph". BEML has received contracts to manufacture 32 B28 trains.Two prototype trains are expected to be ready for trial runs in the first quarter of 2027. BEML informed the BSE on Friday that it has received a separate Rs 5,400-crore contract to manufacture 15 additional B28 trains. The full 508-km Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail corridor is targeted for completion by Dec 2030.

Article Title: Healthcare goes digital: When doctors go behind the app wall, who gets left behind?
Article Text:
Visuals of long queue at Delhi National Cancer Institute (pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

Difficulties patients might face despite digital help

When the smartphone becomes the gateway to healthcare

The Times of India

Nature

Who gets left behind?

ABHA and the push towards connected healthcare

Delhi National Cancer Institute (pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

Insurance goes digital, but payment and paperwork remain a burden

What's the solution?

Covid era showed that systems still struggle

The Times of India

Covid-19 highlights struggle

The Times of India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Digital healthcare cannot mean digital-only healthcare

What if your phone becomes the first thing you need to see a doctor?As healthcare increasingly moves from hospital counters and paper records to apps and online portals, access to care is becoming closely tied to access to technology.For many patients, digital healthcare can mean quicker consultations, easier access to medical records and fewer trips to hospitals. But for others, particularly older people, rural communities, low-income families and those with limited digital literacy, the shift can add another layer of difficulty.The problem is not simply whether a person owns a smartphone. Patients may struggle with internet connectivity, downloading and navigating apps, remembering passwords and OTPs, uploading documents or understanding information presented online.In many households, a single smartphone is shared by several family members, while caregivers often become the bridge between patients and digital health services.As government and private healthcare services increasingly encourage, and in some cases require, people to use digital platforms, a larger question is emerging: Is technology making healthcare more accessible, or creating a new barrier to accessing it?Digital health has opened up several ways for patients to manage their care remotely.People can consult doctors online, monitor blood sugar through connected devices, receive medication and appointment reminders, and access diet and educational resources without making frequent hospital visits.Telemedicine became particularly important during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns made physical consultations difficult. But the experience also exposed how uneven access to digital healthcare could be.A DIG-EQUITY study published in, examining the experiences of people with diabetes, caregivers, healthcare providers, policymakers and community organisations in urban and rural Tamil Nadu, found significant differences in how people used digital health services.Younger patients were generally more comfortable with smartphones, health applications and teleconsultations, while many older people needed family members to book appointments, join consultations or access medical reports.For some, physical limitations added to the problem. Impaired vision or hearing, as well as difficulty handling smartphones, could make navigating digital platforms harder.Even among younger people, digital access did not automatically translate into a preference for online care. Some people with type 1 diabetes continued to prefer in-person consultations because of the need for physical examinations.The digital divide is also closely linked to where people live and what they can afford.Urban patients are more likely to have reliable internet connections, smartphones and access to digital services. A study published in, examining barriers to digital health transformation in India, found that the challenges went beyond simply having a smartphone or internet connection.The study identified poor network coverage and inadequate IT infrastructure, the high cost of devices and digital systems, a lack of technical expertise, language and communication barriers, and difficulties faced by users among the major challenges.For patients, these barriers can have very practical consequences. The study noted that some had to rely on family members' smartphones to attend teleconsultations, while the cost of smart devices could limit access to mobile health applications.The findings suggest that digital access cannot be measured simply by whether someone owns a phone. Reliable connectivity, affordability, digital skills, language accessibility and the availability of human support all influence whether a patient can actually use digital healthcare.That distinction becomes particularly important as healthcare services increasingly move online. Putting a service on a digital platform does not automatically make it accessible to everyone.India's digital health infrastructure is expanding rapidly. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), through platforms such as ABHA, is aimed at creating a connected digital health ecosystem, while eSanjeevani has widened access to telemedicine.With hundreds of millions of ABHA IDs created and telemedicine consultations running into hundreds of millions, the scale of this shift is significant.But the benefits of digital healthcare are not evenly experienced.The gap becomes particularly visible when digital systems are introduced at the hospital level. For some patients, the shift has not removed queues; it has created an additional one.Rekha (name changed), a patient at the Delhi National Cancer Institute, said patients earlier had to wait in a single OPD queue, with doctors arriving around 8am. According to her, the process now involves generating a token through the ABHA app before reaching the hospital, followed by another number at the reception.“Earlier there used to be only one OPD line and the doctors used to arrive at 8am. Now they have made it mandatory to download the ABHA app and apply for a token number. Then we get another number from reception, and doctors arrive at 10am. Several patients need immediate care, but this extra queue has made life a bit more difficult,” she said.For those without a smartphone or reliable internet connection, Rekha said the process can begin hours before they reach the doctor. Some patients, she said, arrive around midnight or 1am and spend the night waiting because they cannot access the network or generate a digital token.Those with smartphones may apply through the ABHA app around 5am and reach the hospital by 7am, she said, only to wait again at reception before seeing a doctor later in the morning.Dr Manisha Arora, Director, Internal Medicine, CK Birla Hospital, Delhi, said ABHA should remain a facilitator rather than become a gateway to treatment.“A patient should never feel that access to technology determines access to healthcare,” she said, noting that patients without an ABHA ID, smartphone or internet connectivity should continue to be able to register physically and receive the same clinical care.She stressed that hospitals should adopt a digital-first, not digital-only, approach.“That means retaining manual registration counters, providing assisted kiosks and having dedicated digital-support personnel, particularly for elderly and first-time users.”Digital insurance processes are another area where patients can struggle. Families dealing with hospitalisation may simultaneously have to navigate e-KYC, pre-authorisation, co-payments, deductions and non-payable items.Manivannan Selvaraj, Founder and Managing Director, Kauvery Group of Hospitals, said translating a clinical treatment plan into a pre-authorisation submission, and then managing the queries and follow-ups that come back, involves a long chain of steps that a patient is neither equipped nor educated to handle, and should not have to handle while they or a family member is unwell.“Sometimes delays or claim issues arise because documentation is incomplete rather than because of a medical concern,” Arora said, stressing that hospital insurance desks need to act as patient counsellors, explaining the process rather than merely uploading documents.“True digital accessibility is when technology works in the background and the patient still experiences a human interface at the front,” she said.At 65, Amarnath (name changed) has an insurance policy but says managing it digitally has become difficult. He is often unsure about when he can claim, when premiums are due and how to complete the process online, leaving his son to handle the details for him.“I have an insurance policy, but I often don’t know when I can make a claim, when the premium is due or how to complete these processes online. My son manages it for me. At my age, it is not always easy to visit a centre every time I need to check my policy or make a claim. If healthcare is becoming digital, these services should also be made accessible to elderly people, so that we can manage them ourselves without having to depend on others,” he said.He also highlighted how the growing use of digital payments in hospitals can create another challenge for elderly patients unfamiliar with the technology. Having a UPI-enabled phone does not necessarily mean being comfortable using it, particularly during a medical emergency when payments may need to be made quickly.“I have UPI on my phone, but for people of our generation, it is difficult to become fully comfortable with the process and make an immediate payment, especially during a health emergency. This is something that should also be addressed,” he said.The pandemic offered an early and stark example of how closely technology and healthcare had become intertwined.While telemedicine and digital systems helped patients access services during lockdowns, other parts of the healthcare chain showed that digitisation alone could not solve problems of capacity and access.As reported byearlier, delays in Covid testing became a major concern during the second wave. Udham Singh, 22, developed high fever, severe cough, body ache and breathlessness after his sample was collected for an RT-PCR test. His report, which confirmed Covid infection, came several days after the sample was taken.“I would have landed in an ICU had I waited for some more time. The element of uncertainty due to delay also caused extreme mental trauma,” Singh said.For patients waiting at home, the delay was not merely an inconvenience. It affected decisions about treatment and isolation. Some families also faced difficulties maintaining quarantine while waiting for test results.Priya Jaiswal, a resident of Old Delhi, recalled how a network outage during the pandemic left her dependent on officials for essential medicines. With her internet connection down, she could not use UPI to make payments or order medicines online, leaving her waiting for officials to arrive at her home.“We had to wait for hours for officials to arrive and hand over the medicines while we were in quarantine. Even online consultations became difficult because of continuous power cuts at a time when we needed healthcare the most,” she said.The surge in demand for Covid testing also put pressure on government laboratories to issue digital reports on time, highlighting another challenge for digital healthcare: a digital interface is only as effective as the system supporting it.Covid-19 vaccination certificates also affected people's travel and employment plans.Varghese Thomas, a youth from the city, told TOI that five people in his group had taken their first vaccine dose around the same time, but only one had received the certificate nearly 40 days later.“When we applied for jobs, prospective employers were asking us about the vaccination. They wanted us to produce the certificate,” he said.Registering through Co-WIN was another difficulty for people in rural areas.As reported byearlier, 68-year-old Adhi Kesavan from Gudiyattam in Tamil Nadu's Vellore district had to travel around 5-7 km with his wife to a common service centre to register for vaccination.Kesavan did not own a smartphone or know how to use one. He was directed to the centre by his panchayat head, who told him that his details could be registered there and that the hospital would contact him when a vaccine became available.“I heard from our panchayat head that we can get vaccinated if we register at the e-sevai maiyyam. Our number will be given to the hospitals nearby and we will get a call once the vaccine is ready,” Kesavan said.He was still waiting for that call.India's digital-health expansion will ultimately be measured not only by how many people are connected to the system, but also by whether those who are not can still access care with the same ease and dignity.The goal should not be to make healthcare digital at any cost. It should be to make healthcare more accessible, using technology when it helps, and providing human support when it doesn't.Because for a patient struggling to connect, navigate an app, remember an OTP or make a digital payment, the smartphone should never become another obstacle between them and a doctor.
Article Summary: Digital health has opened up several ways for patients to manage their care remotely. People can consult doctors online, monitor blood sugar through connected devices, and access diet and educational resources without making frequent hospital visits. But for others, particularly older people, rural communities, low-income families and those with limited digital literacy, the shift can add another layer of difficulty.

NEW DELHI: The law ministry has notified the appointment of 14 new judges to four high courts, which include Delhi, Karnataka, Jharkhand, and J&K and Ladakh. Article Title: Yemeni national attacks Sikh bus driver in Telford, smashes & hijacks vehicle

LONDON: A 33-year-old Yemeni national was arrested for allegedly assaulting a British Sikh bus driver, vandalising the vehicle, hijacking it and crashing the bus into multiple vehicles in Telford, in England’s West Midlands region, last week.The unprovoked attack occurred around 6.37pm at Court Street in Madeley, Shropshire, on Sept 18. Video footage shared by a bystander showed the accused, Ali Balhad, grabbing the driver, punching him and tugging at his beard. The attacker was seen pulling out the cash register and hurling it at the driver.Throughout the ordeal, the driver appeared calm, holding on to his beard and begging people around to call the police. “Just take this guy away from me,” he was heard saying.To distract the attacker, Kymberlee Daley (19), who filmed the assault, told him that she had called the police, allowing the driver to jump out of the bus window and flee. To her horror, Balhad took the wheel and started driving the single-decker bus the wrong way down the street.The bus collided with multiple vehicles before coming to a stop, even as shocked bystanders chased it.Armed officers arrived at the scene within 10 minutes and arrested Balhad, who had been in Telford for about a week. He was charged with aggravated vehicle taking; assault; attempted grievous bodily harm; driving a motor vehicle dangerously; robbery; theft from a store; threats to kill; and three counts of criminal damage. The accused was remanded in custody and is due to appear before Telford Magistrates’ Court Monday.Paramedics treated the bus driver for minor injuries, West Mercia police said.

Article Title: Punjab CM launches 'Mann Da Munafa' door-to-door campaign highlighting welfare initiatives

Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann on Sunday launched the AAP's door-to-door election campaign for the 2027 Punjab assembly polls, pitching his government's 'Mann Da Munafa' narrative, claiming that every family is receiving an annual benefit of Rs 1.82 lakh from its welfare initiatives like free electricity and healthcare.Mann said the AAP would go to every household with its record of work undertaken since 2022, while asserting that the campaign would remain positive and focus on what the government has delivered for Punjab.He said the AAP would seek people's support based on the work delivered on the ground and question the opposition over its record and the issue of combating drugs.During the outreach, Mann went door-to-door in Dhuri, met several families and interacted with elderly residents, women, youngsters and children.He listened to their views, discussed the work undertaken by the government over the past four-and-a-half years and explained how various schemes and initiatives were translating into direct benefits for ordinary households."Every family in Punjab is today benefiting by Rs 1.82 lakh annually from the initiatives rolled out by our government. This is not an abstract figure. It represents money a household no longer has to take out of its own pocket for electricity, healthcare, education and other essential services," he said."I want every family to sit down and calculate for itself how much it is saving every month. That is the real meaning of 'Mann Da Munafa'," Mann added.Claiming that his welfare initiatives reduced the financial burden of essential services on families, the chief minister said the government allowed them to use their hard-earned money for other household needs."Free electricity, healthcare, education, and Maavan Dheeyan Satkar Yojna are helping people save their hard-earned money. Lakhs of households across Punjab are receiving zero electricity bills, which means that money that earlier went towards electricity charges can now be spent on children, homes and farms," he said."The expansion of primary healthcare has also meant that a fever, a check-up or a basic diagnostic test does not have to force a family to borrow money or dip into its savings," Mann added.He said improvements in government schools have given parents greater confidence to educate their children without the burden of private fees."For decades, the people of Punjab paid taxes without receiving facilities in proportion to what they contributed. Our government is working to close that gap by directing resources towards households rather than privilege," the CM said."Mann Da Munafa is a simple question for every family: how much better off is your household today than it was before? Calculate what you save every month, and that answer will speak louder than any campaign speech," he said.Speaking about rural development, Mann said his government changed how resources were allocated to villages and made village-level development a central part of its approach.On the campaign strategy, he said AAP would keep its election campaign focused on its governance record rather than personal attacks or negativity."Our entire election campaign will remain positive. We will talk only about our work. We will place our record before the people and let them judge it, rather than build a campaign on abuse and negativity," he said."Our workers and candidates will carry the same message into every constituency: the savings delivered to families, the villages developed and public money spent on public welfare," he added.He said the door-to-door outreach provided the most direct opportunity for political representatives to account for their work before the people, adding that the campaign would be taken across Punjab, with party workers and candidates presenting the government's record directly before households.On the opposition, Mann said, "Congress is fighting among itself in Punjab, with its leaders more occupied with internal contests than with the concerns of the people, while the Shiromani Akali Dal has been wiped out and no longer commands a presence on the ground."On the issue of drugs, Mann questioned the BJP's position, claiming that drugs are being brought into Punjab from Gujarat."With what face is the BJP talking about drugs when it is bringing drugs into Punjab from Gujarat, he asked. PTI

Article Title: BJP, Congress trade barbs over PM Modi mimicry at Rahul Gandhi’s Indore event
Article Text:
PM Modi mimicry at Rahul Gandhi event

BJP leaders hit out at Rahul Gandhi
